loop/x: Here is one full training step for a tiny linear classifier, with two features and two classes. The input x is two, one, and the correct class is class zero.
loop/scores: Forward: the scores are W x plus b, one per class: one, and one point eight five.
loop/probs: Softmax turns them into probabilities, zero point three and zero point seven. The model leans the wrong way.
loop/grad: Backward: the gradient on the scores is p minus the one-hot label, minus zero point seven and plus zero point seven.
loop/update: Then every weight and bias steps against its own gradient. What is left is to find those gradients.
outer/chain: Score i is row i of W dotted with x, plus b i. So nudging the weight W i j moves score i by x j times as much.
outer/outer: By the chain rule, the gradient on W i j is ds i times x j. Every entry of ds times every entry of x: an outer product.
outer/db: Each bias adds straight into its own score, so its gradient is just ds.
toward/step: Now step, here with eta one half. Row zero belongs to the correct class, and its ds is minus zero point seven, so it gains zero point three five times x: it moves toward x.
toward/away: Row one, the wrong class, has ds plus zero point seven. It loses zero point three five times x, and moves away.
toward/scores: Measured along x, the correct row climbs from one to two point seven five, and the wrong one falls from one point eight five to zero point one.
example/ask: Your turn. The weight in row one, column zero is one. The input is three, minus one; the correct class is class one; softmax gives zero point four and zero point six; and eta is zero point one. What is that weight after one step?
example/ds: The score gradient, p minus one-hot, is zero point four, and zero point six minus one: minus zero point four.
example/dW: The weight's gradient is ds one times x zero: minus zero point four times three, minus one point two.
example/step: Step against it: one, minus zero point one times minus one point two, is one point one two. The correct class's weight grew.
